1950: a name for a house in Kåbo
The word arrived before the concrete.The Swedish architect Hans Asplundcoined the term nybrutalism — newbrutalism — to describe Villa Göth, amodern brick home in Uppsala.
The house was designed in January 1950by Bengt Edman and Lennart Holm,contemporaries of Asplund. Nothingabout it was monumental.
What it showed was the "as found" approach thatwould later sit at the core of brutalism: thebuilding was allowed to say what it was made of,and no finish was added to soften the answer.
Villa Göth was listed as historically significantby the Uppsala county board on 3 March 1995 — thehouse that named the movement outlived most ofthe towers built in its name.
poured concrete keeping thetongue-and-groove pattern of its forms
English architects visiting Sweden — MichaelVentris, Oliver Cox, Graeme Shankland — carrythe term home, where it "spread like wildfire".
Alison Smithson puts "new brutalism" in printfor the first time, describing the unbuilt Sohohouse in Architectural Design.
Hunstanton School completes in Norfolk: thefirst finished building in the world its ownarchitects called "new brutalist".
The Sugden House completes in Watford.Hunstanton was likely inspired by Mies van derRohe's 1946 Alumni Memorial Hall in Chicago.
It is our intention inthis building to have thestructure exposedentirely, withoutinterior finisheswherever practicable.
Reyner Banham, Britisharchitectural historian, used"new brutalism" to identify bothan ethic and an aesthetic in his1955 essay The New Brutalism.
He named Hunstanton and the Sohohouse as "the reference by whichThe New Brutalism inarchitecture may be defined".
He expanded the argument in his1966 book The New Brutalism:Ethic or Aesthetic?

"if there is one single verbal formula that has made theconcept of Brutalism admissible in most of the world'sWestern languages, it is that Le Corbusier himselfdescribed that concrete work as 'béton-brut'"

New brutalism was never only a style. It was a philosophicalapproach to design — a striving to create simple, honest,functional buildings that accommodate their purpose,inhabitants and location, a strict modernist language setagainst the retrospective nostalgia of much 1940s architecture.

Peter Smithson held that the core of brutalism was a reverencefor materials, expressed honestly: "Brutalism is not concernedwith the material as such but rather the quality of material",and "the seeing of materials for what they were: the woodnessof the wood; the sandiness of sand".

John Voelcker said the new brutalism "cannot be understoodthrough stylistic analysis, although some day a comprehensiblestyle might emerge" — supporting the Smithsons' description ofthe movement as an ethic, not an aesthetic.
valuation of materials fortheir inherent qualities
Banham also required the aesthetic"image" — the coherence of thebuilding as a visual entity.
The grain of the formwork stays in the wall

Raw concrete is often used because of its lowcost, and then left to reveal the basic natureof its construction — rough surfaces carryingthe wood "shuttering" pattern produced whenthe forms were cast in situ.
The style commonly uses exposed, unpaintedconcrete or brick, angular geometric shapesand a predominantly monochrome colour palette;steel, timber and glass also feature.
Examples are frequently massive in charactereven when not large, and challenge traditionalnotions of what a building should look like,with focus given to interior spaces as much asexterior.
Buildings are constructed with recurringmodular elements representing specificfunctional zones, distinctly articulatedand grouped into a unified whole.
Emphasis falls on graphic expression inthe external elevations and in thewhole-site plan, in regard to the mainfunctions and people-flows of thebuilding.
A façade that admits what it is doing
A common theme is the exposure of the building's inner workings — structure,services and human use — on the exterior.

Boston City Hall, designed in 1962: the strikinglydifferent and projected portions of the buildingindicate the special nature of the rooms behind thosewalls, such as the mayor's office or the city councilchambers.

Hunstanton School put the facility's water tank —normally a hidden service feature — in aprominent, visible tower. Its water and electricutilities were delivered via readily visiblepipes and conduits rather than hidden in thewalls.
Concrete was the point, not the compromise

Brutalism as an architectural philosophy was often associatedwith a socialist utopian ideology, supported by its designersand especially by Alison and Peter Smithson near the height ofthe style. Their work sought to connect architecture with whatthey saw as the realities of modern life.

Among their early contributions were "streets in the sky", inwhich traffic and pedestrian circulation were rigorouslyseparated — a theme popular in the 1960s. In Britain the stylefeatured in utilitarian, low-cost social housing influenced bysocialist principles, and spread from there to other regions.
In Czechoslovakia it was presented as an attempt at a"national" but also "modern socialist" style; suchprefabricated socialist-era buildings are called panelaky.
Brick brutalism, or"brickalism", is the sub-genrewhere brick dominates insteadof concrete — from theSmithsons' Soho house (1952)to Colin St John Wilson'sBritish Library (1982–1998).

The universities built them first, and biggest
The 'beehives' at St John's College,Oxford (Michael Powers, Architects' Co-Partnership, 1958–60).
The 1959 architecture departmentextension at Cambridge under LeslieMartin, by Colin St John Wilson and AlexHardy with student participation — itinspired the Grade II listed UniversityCentre.

Stirling's Red Trilogy: LeicesterEngineering with James Gowan (1959–63),often called Britain's first postmodernbuilding; the Grade II* History Faculty,Cambridge (1964–67); the FloreyBuilding, Oxford (1966–71).
Basil Spence's Grade I Falmer House atSussex (1960–62), a “meeting of Arts andCrafts with modernism” — hand-madebricks and colonnades of board-markedconcrete arches inspired by theColosseum.
(1968): six linked halls in NorfolkTerrace, four in Suffolk Terrace, withthe library and teaching wall betweenthem.
Ove Arup's Grade I Kingsgate Bridge atDurham (1963) and Dunelm House(1964–66), saved from demolition in 2021after a five-year campaign.
Paul Rudolph's Art and ArchitectureBuilding at Yale (1963), where asdepartment chair he was both client andarchitect. His 1964 UMass Dartmouth is arare entire campus in the style.
William Pereira's Geisel Library at UCSan Diego (1969–70), “a fascinatingnexus between brutalism and futurism” —intended in steel and glass until costmoved the structure outside.
Robarts Library, Toronto (Warner, Burns,Toan and Lunde, 1968–73), condemned onopening as “a blunder on the grandestscale”.
The UEA ziggurats closed in 2023 in the reinforced autoclaved aeratedconcrete crisis, with no refurbishment date set as of February 2025.
The Western City Gate — also known as the Genex Tower — in Belgrade, Serbia.
Formed by two towers connected with a two-storey bridge, with a revolving restaurant atthe top. With the restaurant it reaches135–140 m (443–459 ft).
Considered a prime representative of the stylein Serbia, and one of the best built anywherein the 1960s and 1970s.
The source calls the Genex Tower thesecond-tallest high-rise in Belgrade,after Ušće Tower — but gives no heightfor it. The gap is printed, not estimated.
Few styles in history can have been metwith so many pleas from its users tosee it destroyed.
A 2014 article in The Economist noted that a campaign to demolish a buildingwill usually be directed against a brutalist one.
In 2005 the British TV programme Demolition ran apublic vote to select twelve buildings that ought tobe demolished — eight of those selected werebrutalist.
Concrete façades do not age well in damp maritime climates:water stains, moss and lichen, rust from the reinforcing bars.Critics add the "cold" look and an air of totalitarianism.
The Queen Elizabeth Square flatsin Glasgow (1962) were demolishedin 1993.

The original movement was largely over bythe late 1970s and early 1980s, havinggiven way to structural expressionism anddeconstructivism. Interest resurged from2015, and new construction followed,termed neobrutalism.
Wang Shu's Ningbo Museum (2008) showstraces of the bamboo framework on itsmonumental concrete, called "an urbanicon" in his 2012 Pritzker Prizecitation.
The campus of the private University ofEngineering and Technology (UTEC) inPeru, by Yvonne Farrell and ShelleyMcNamara, is referenced in their 2020Pritzker citation.

Neobrutalist buildings tend to be commissioned by theprivate sector, and may use recycled brick or timber ratherthan concrete — while still exposing materials and structure.

Many defining aspects have been softened: façades sandblastedto a stone-like surface, covered in stucco, or made ofpatterned precast elements — as in the redevelopment ofSheffield's Park Hill. But board-marked concrete is stillused, as at the neobrutalist Silberrad Student Centre,University of Essex (2015).
Judge it the way itasked to be judged

The style has been polarising throughout its history — public campaigns to demolishbrutalist buildings are common, and in the United Kingdom some have been preserved.
